kurz: How the saver's allowance keeps €1,000 of capital income a year tax-free, and why the exemption order has to be held by the bank where the income arises.

bloecke.md:
The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is governed by Section 20(9) EStG (Income Tax Act). Under it, €1,000 of capital income a year remains tax-free, or €2,000 for spouses assessed jointly. These amounts have applied since 2023 and remain unchanged in 2026. Before that, the allowance stood at €801 for fourteen years. The increase of just under a quarter has not made up for the loss of purchasing power since 2009.

Formally, the saver's allowance is a lump-sum allowance for income-related expenses (Werbungskosten) that takes the place of the costs actually incurred. The wording of the law expressly rules out deducting those costs. Custody fees, specialist literature, stock market newsletters and advisory fees therefore do not reduce the tax base, not even through the most-favourable assessment (Günstigerprüfung). With €3,000 of income and €400 of custody costs, €2,000 is taxable.

The allowance is not taken into account automatically when tax is withheld. Without an exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag), the bank withholds capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) from the first cent. The money is not lost, but it sits with the tax office, earning no interest, until the next tax return.

## Order of the calculation steps

Two calculation steps come before the allowance. First, the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) reduces the tax base for funds: by 30% for equity funds, 15% for mixed funds and 60% or 80% for real estate funds. The bank then offsets the balances of the loss pots against the income. Only then is the allowance applied to the amount that remains.

For an equity fund, the allowance therefore covers €1,428.57 of gross income and not just €1,000, because only 70% of it enters the tax base. For interest from an instant-access savings account, it is exactly €1,000, because there is no partial exemption there. The same order applies to the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]]: first the partial exemption is deducted, then the allowance.

bloecke.formel: Taxable = Gross income × (1 − Partial exemption) − Losses offset − Allowance
bloecke.erklaerung: The partial exemption is deducted before the allowance. For equity funds, the allowance therefore covers more gross income than for interest.
variablen: distribution, advance lump sum or capital gain

bloecke.md: Only the base interest rate is official. It is 3.20% as of 2 January 2026 and is the highest value since the advance lump sum was introduced. This gives a base return (Basisertrag) of 2.24% of the value at the start of the year, of which 1.568% is taxable after the 30% partial exemption. A tax base of €1,000 therefore requires a fund value of €63,800. With the distributing ETF, the distribution of 1.7% is below the base return. An advance lump sum of 0.54% is therefore added, provided the unit value rises by at least 0.54% during the year. The taxable amount is then also 1.568%, and the same €63,800 is sufficient. The advance lump sum for a given year is only deemed received on the first working day of the following year, for 2026 on 4 January 2027, and therefore counts against the following year's allowance. If the base interest rate stays the same, this does not change the annual total. The interest and distribution rates of the other bars are assumptions in line with typical market levels, not a forecast.

## The exemption order

The order is issued separately for each bank using the officially prescribed form and is invalid without the tax identification number (Section 44a(2a) EStG). The total of all orders may not exceed €1,000 or €2,000 as applicable. This is checked centrally, not by the individual bank. Each institution reports to the Federal Central Tax Office (BZSt) the amount of capital income it has exempted; the legal basis is Section 45d EStG in conjunction with Section 93c AO (Fiscal Code), and the deadline is the end of February of the following year. Any double use is spotted there and leads to a demand for back tax.

An exemption order issued during the year takes effect retroactively from 1 January. The bank refunds tax already withheld with the next settlement. For the year just ended, an order can still be issued or increased until 31 January. The bank must then correct the tax deduction if it has not yet produced the tax certificate. Otherwise, as a rule, the only remaining route is the capital income annex (Anlage KAP). The unused part of the allowance lapses and can neither be carried forward to the following year nor carried back to the previous year.

bloecke.titel: Splitting the allowance across three banks (illustrative calculation, 2026 base interest rate)

bloecke.md: The table shows the difficulty that the split has to be estimated in advance. In the example, €9.60 of the exemption amount remains unused at Bank B, while €9.60 too much is taxed at Bank C. That is €2.53 of tax that can only be recovered through the capital income annex. With larger misestimates, three-figure amounts are at stake. If it becomes clear in November how the income is distributed, the orders can still be changed for the current year.

The tax on the advance lump sum is debited automatically from the settlement account in the first days of January, often before investors are thinking about taxes. If the exemption order is only issued in spring, the tax on this item has already been paid. The bank must correct this as long as the tax certificate for the year has not yet been issued (Section 44b(5) EStG). The advance lump sum for 2026 is charged in January 2027. With a base interest rate of 3.20%, it carries noticeable weight even in smaller portfolios.

## Spouses

Spouses assessed jointly receive a joint allowance of €2,000. Half of it is deducted for each spouse. If one of them stays below €1,000, the unused part passes automatically to the other (Section 20(9) sentences 2 and 3 EStG). If one spouse has €1,800 of income and the other €100, no tax is due.

For withholding at source, however, this only applies with a joint exemption order. It covers joint accounts as well as both spouses' individual accounts at that institution. In addition, it allows the bank to offset one spouse's losses against the other's gains. Conversely, an individual order does not apply to a joint securities account. Unmarried couples cannot use these rules, because the allowance is strictly tied to the individual. A joint securities account does not change this either.

## The non-assessment certificate (NV-Bescheinigung)

If taxable income is below the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag), which in 2026 is €12,348, or €24,696 for joint assessment, the exemption order does not go far enough. In that case, the tax office for your place of residence issues a non-assessment certificate (Nichtveranlagungsbescheinigung) on application (form NV 1 A). It is submitted to the bank and exempts all capital income from deduction, not just the first €1,000. It is issued subject to revocation, is valid for at most three years and always ends at the end of a calendar year (Section 44a(2) EStG). Typical cases are students, pensioners with a small pension and children. If income rises above the basic tax-free allowance, the tax office must be informed.

## Children's securities accounts

A child is a taxpayer in their own right, with their own basic tax-free allowance, their own saver's allowance and their own lump-sum allowance for special expenses (Sonderausgaben-Pauschbetrag) of €36 (Section 10c EStG). Arithmetically, this means that €13,384 of capital income a year remains tax-free, provided the child has no other income and a non-assessment certificate is in place. This is the basis for the legal option of spreading family wealth across children's securities accounts. At this order of magnitude, that is worth considerably more than the parents' allowance.

This arrangement has three limits, none of which is a tax limit. The transfer is final. The securities account belongs to the child, the parents merely manage it, and from the age of 18 the child alone has control over it. If the parents later take the money back for their own purposes, they risk the tax office no longer recognising the attribution of the income to the child at all.

bloecke.titel: Child benefit without an income limit
bloecke.md: Child benefit (Kindergeld) has been independent of income since 2012. The former income limit for adult children in education or training no longer exists; the objection to children's securities accounts comes from old guidebooks. The limits for health insurance and BAföG, on the other hand, still apply.

## Using up the allowance with price gains

If current income is not enough to use up the allowance, the allowance can be topped up with realised price gains. To do this, securities are sold and immediately bought back. In its judgment of 25 August 2009 (IX R 60/07), the Federal Fiscal Court (BFH) did not regard a sale with a same-day repurchase of securities of the same kind as an abuse of legal arrangements (Gestaltungsmissbrauch). Economically, nothing changes, but for tax purposes the acquisition costs rise. The gain realised tax-free today therefore no longer falls into the tax base later. The tax is thus saved permanently and not merely deferred, provided the position is ultimately sold at a gain at all.

Three restrictions apply. The allowance must still be available, trading costs the spread and an order fee, and the [[FIFO]] principle changes the order of the purchases. The repurchase is recorded as the newest tranche in the securities account, while in a later partial sale the oldest units continue to be sold first.

The starting point is an equity ETF worth €20,000 with a book gain of €4,000. This year, €200 of interest has already arisen as current income. This leaves €800 of the allowance still available.

Because of the partial exemption, a gross gain of 800 ÷ 0.7 = €1,142.86 is needed to use up this remainder. That is around 29% of the position, or about €5,720 in order volume. The costs are two orders at €1 each plus a spread of around 0.04% (€2.30), €4.30 in total. The tax saving is 800 × 26.375% = €211.00. Without a partial exemption, for example with an individual share, exactly €800 of gain would have to be realised.

If you forget the partial exemption in the calculation, you realise too little gain and let part of the allowance lapse.

bloecke.titel: Cost of an allowance left unused year after year
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with €263.75 of tax overpaid per year (€1,000 × 26.375%), reinvested at 6% at the end of each year.

bloecke.md:
- The exemption order was never issued. The bank then deducts tax from the first cent, and this tax can only be recovered through the tax return.
- The order is held by the wrong bank, for example the one with the instant-access savings account, while the income arises in the securities account.
- The order remains in place at a closed account and continues to block part of the exemption amount there.
- The orders add up to more than €1,000. The cross-check at the Federal Central Tax Office reveals this, and a demand for back tax follows.
- Income-related expenses are claimed, even though Section 20(9) sentence 1 EStG rules out their deduction without exception.
- The allowance is not used up. It lapses without replacement on 31 December every year.

mitnehmen: The tax-free amount is €1,000 per person per year, or €2,000 for spouses assessed jointly; without any tax being deducted, this only works with an exemption order at the bank where the income arises.
The partial exemption is deducted before the allowance, so that for an equity fund the allowance covers €1,428.57 of gross income, and for interest exactly €1,000.
The allowance lapses at the end of the year; any remainder that current income does not fill can be used by deliberately taking profits, bearing in mind costs and the FIFO order.
With income below the basic tax-free allowance, the non-assessment certificate goes further than the exemption order, because it exempts all capital income and not just €1,000.
Children's securities accounts are attractive for tax purposes, but they are limited by family insurance, BAföG and the final transfer of the money to the child.

begriffe.text: Lump-sum deduction for income-related expenses on income from capital assets under Section 20(9) EStG, amounting to €1,000 per person per year, or €2,000 for spouses assessed jointly. It rules out deducting the income-related expenses actually incurred.

Instruction to a bank to exempt capital income up to a specified amount from tax deduction. It is issued per institution and is only valid with the tax identification number (Section 44a(2a) EStG). The total of all orders is limited to the allowance and is cross-checked by the Federal Central Tax Office.

Certificate from the tax office for the place of residence (form NV 1 A) for people whose taxable income stays below the basic tax-free allowance. It exempts all capital income from tax deduction, is valid for at most three years and is subject to revocation (Section 44a(2) EStG).

Order issued by both spouses for up to €2,000. It applies to joint accounts and to both spouses' individual accounts at the same institution, and allows the bank to offset one spouse's losses against the other's gains.
